title: Dzongu Lepcha Homestays: How to Stay in the Reserve
meta_description: Staying with Lepcha families in Dzongu: villages, the Dzongu permit, costs of ₹1,800–2,500 a day with meals, getting there from Mangan, and house manners.
summary: Dzongu, the Lepcha reserve across the Teesta from Mangan, has no hotels, only family homestays in villages such as Lingthem, Passingdang and Hee Gyathang. Expect about ₹1,800–2,500 per person a day with all meals. You need a Dzongu permit, usually arranged in Mangan. Bridges and roads changed after 2023; check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Why stay in Dzongu
paras: Most visitors to North Sikkim spend three days in a jeep chasing snow and a lake at 5,000 m. Dzongu is the opposite trip. You cross the Teesta at Sankalang below Mangan into a valley of terraced paddy, cardamom under alder trees, waterfalls and old forest that runs up toward Khangchendzonga National Park, and you stay put. For two or three nights you live with a Lepcha family, eat what they eat, and walk to the next village or the nearest waterfall.

Dzongu matters because it is a reserve. The Lepchas, Mutanchi Rongkup in their own language, are regarded as Sikkim's first people, and Dzongu was set aside for them in the time of the Chogyals. Land here is held by Dzongu Lepchas, outsiders need a permit to enter, and there are no hotels. The homestays are how the valley chooses to welcome guests, and staying in one puts money straight into Lepcha households.

The flood of October 2023, when South Lhonak lake burst and the Teesta rose through the valley, damaged the river bridges that link Dzongu to Mangan, including the crossing at Sankalang. Temporary crossings and diversions have kept the villages reachable much of the time, but not always. Ask your hosts how to come that week and check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Villages and what each is known for
paras: Dzongu is divided informally into lower and upper parts. Homestays are spread across a dozen villages; these are the ones visitors reach most often. Distances and road conditions changed after the 2023 flood damaged bridges on the Teesta, so ask your hosts how to come that week.

sections.heading: What a homestay is like
paras: Dzongu homestays are family houses with two to five guest rooms. Some are newer concrete houses; others are traditional Lepcha houses of wood and bamboo raised on stone. Rooms are simple and clean, with thick quilts, and bathrooms may be attached or shared, with hot water by geyser or bucket. Power cuts happen, and mobile signal is patchy, with BSNL and Jio working in some villages and not others.

All meals are included and cooked by the family: rice, dal, greens from the garden, squash, ferns, nettle soup, sometimes river fish or chicken, and a sharp chilli relish. Hosts often offer chi, the millet drink served in bamboo. Many families also guide you on village walks, to waterfalls, to hot springs or to the monastery, for a modest fee.

Mayal Lyang Homestay in Lingthem is one of the longest-running and is often the first contact for visitors. Many other families host guests; book directly by phone or through a Gangtok contact you trust, and ask whether the price includes all meals and the permit help.

Bring a torch, a light fleece for the evenings, sandals for the house, insect repellent, and any medicines you need; the nearest pharmacy is in Mangan. A small gift from home, such as sweets or tea, is welcome but never expected.

sections.heading: Costs and permits
paras: Dzongu is good value compared with a North Sikkim package. Indicative 2025–26 prices for budget travel are below. The permit is the part to sort first: it has usually been issued by the district administration in Mangan, and many homestays arrange it if you send ID copies and photographs a few days ahead. Whether foreign nationals may enter has varied over the years. Check current status before you travel.
list: Homestay with all meals: about ₹1,800–2,500 per person per day.
Shared jeep Gangtok (Vajra stand) to Mangan: ₹200–300 a seat, about 3 hours.
Taxi from Mangan to a Dzongu village: ₹800–1,500 a car.
Reserved car Gangtok to a Dzongu village: ₹3,500–5,000 one way.
Local guide for a village or waterfall walk: ₹500–1,000 a day.
Dzongu permit: small fee or free.
Three nights door to door from Gangtok, shared jeep and taxi: roughly ₹7,500–10,000 per person.

sections.heading: Things to do in two or three days
paras: Dzongu rewards slowness. Walk from your village to the next along footpaths between paddy and cardamom, with your host or a young guide from the village. Visit the waterfalls, which are fullest after the monsoon in September and October. Ask to see a cardamom drying shed in autumn, or the rice harvest in November. Lingthem's monastery and the small village gompas are open to respectful visitors.

In a Kamsel year, Tholung Monastery in upper Dzongu brings out relics hidden there during the Gorkha invasions; the display falls in April, once every three years, and draws pilgrims from across Sikkim. In any season, ask your hosts about Lepcha lore: how the first man and woman were shaped from the snows of Kongchen Konglo, Kanchenjunga, and why the mountain is the Lepchas' guardian. Bring time, not an itinerary.

sections.heading: A sample three-night stay
paras: This is the plan we give friends who want a first taste of Dzongu without rushing. It assumes a homestay in Lingthem or a nearby village, shared transport from Gangtok, and dry weather between October and April. Adjust the walks to your host's suggestions; they know which paths and bridges are in good shape that season.

Leave Gangtok early on the first day, because the shared jeeps from Vajra stand fill fastest in the morning and you still need the permit in Mangan. Most people arrive at the homestay by mid-afternoon, in time for tea, a walk around the house and the fields, and an early dinner by the kitchen fire. Expect the evening to be quiet: no television in many houses, few shops, and stars over the valley if the sky is clear.

On the last morning, eat breakfast, settle the bill in cash, and leave by 9 or 10 am so you reach Mangan in time for a shared jeep back to Gangtok. If you are going on to Lachung or Lachen, remember that the North Sikkim tour starts from Gangtok, not Mangan, and needs its own permit filed a day ahead.
list: Day 1: shared jeep Gangtok to Mangan, permit, taxi to the village, afternoon walk, dinner with the family.
Day 2: guided walk to a waterfall and the next village, lunch at home, afternoon at the monastery or in the fields.
Day 3: a longer walk or a rest day; ask to watch or help with cooking, weaving or the harvest.
Day 4: breakfast, taxi to Mangan, shared jeep back to Gangtok, arriving by mid-afternoon.

sections.heading: House manners and good practice
paras: You are a guest in someone's home inside a protected homeland. These small things make the stay go well for everyone.
list: Take off your shoes when entering the house and the kitchen.
Ask before photographing people, rituals and the inside of shrines.
Dress modestly in villages and at monasteries.
Do not pick plants, flowers or cardamom without asking.
Carry your waste back out; there is no municipal collection.
Pay in cash; UPI often fails without signal.

faqs.q: How much does a Dzongu homestay cost?
faqs.a: About ₹1,800–2,500 per person per day, including three home-cooked meals, in 2025–26. Guided walks cost ₹500–1,000 a day extra, and the taxi from Mangan ₹800–1,500. Three nights door to door from Gangtok by shared jeep and taxi comes to roughly ₹7,500–10,000 per person. Prices are indicative.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Dzongu?
faqs.a: Yes. Everyone who is not a Dzongu resident needs a Dzongu permit, usually issued by the district administration in Mangan. Many homestays arrange it if you send ID copies and photographs ahead. It does not cover Lachung or Lachen. Check current status before you travel.

It has varied. Foreign nationals have been allowed into Dzongu at some times and restricted at others. Ask your homestay and the Mangan district office well before you plan, and check current status before you travel. Foreigners can visit Mangan and Singhik with the general Sikkim entry permit.

faqs.q: How do I reach Dzongu from Gangtok?
faqs.a: Take a shared jeep from Vajra taxi stand to Mangan, ₹200–300 and about 3 hours, then a taxi across the Teesta to your village for ₹800–1,500. Many homestays send a car to Mangan. A reserved car from Gangtok costs ₹3,500–5,000 one way. Ask your hosts about bridges and roads that week.

faqs.q: Which is the best village to stay in Dzongu?
faqs.a: Lingthem is the easiest first choice, with long-running homestays such as Mayal Lyang, a monastery and waterfall walks. Passingdang is closest to Mangan. Hee Gyathang has fine terraced fields. Tingvong and the upper villages are quieter and closer to Tholung. All are good; pick by the host, not the village.

faqs.q: Is Dzongu good for families with children?
faqs.a: Yes. Dzongu sits at about 700–2,000 m, so there is no altitude risk, the walks are short and the food is simple. Children enjoy farm animals, rivers and the freedom of a village. Expect basic bathrooms, power cuts and leeches in the monsoon, and bring a torch.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Dzongu?
faqs.a: October to April, when days are dry and clear. October and November bring harvests and full waterfalls; December to February are mild for walking. April has rhododendrons higher up and, every third year, the Tholung Kamsel. The monsoon months are wet, slippery and full of leeches.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network in Dzongu?
faqs.a: Patchy. BSNL and Jio work in some villages and parts of others, and not at all in places. Tell family you may be out of contact, download maps offline and carry cash, since UPI often fails. Your homestay usually knows the spot in the village where signal is best.

faqs.q: Can I combine Dzongu with Lachung or Lachen?
faqs.a: Yes, and we often suggest it: two or three nights in Dzongu, then back to Gangtok for a North Sikkim tour, or the tour first. You need separate permits for Dzongu and for Lachung or Lachen. Tours start from Gangtok, so plan the order around permit days and road status.
